title: The "patient journey" that isn't a journey at all.
excerpt: A journey implies direction. Someone walking alongside you. But what most patients get is a maze with no map!
body:
PATIENT EXPERIENCE · CLINICAL LEADERSHIP

A journey implies direction. Someone walking alongside you. But what most patients get is a maze with no map!

Here’s what the data, and the front desk, are actually telling us.

6 MIN READ
PATIENT EXPERIENCE
GCC HEALTHCARE

A patient walks into a clinic. In their head, a thousand anxious questions are already rolling: Is it serious? Will I understand what they tell me? Can I afford this?

Then the healthcare system does what it does best: it makes things worse.

  • No clear signage.
  • A walk from one desk to another, then another.
  • A form asking for the same information they gave five minutes ago at the last counter.
  • A wait with no estimated time, no update, no acknowledgment.
  • An eight-minute consultation for a problem they’ve carried for eight weeks.
  • Discharge instructions handed over in language they can barely read, let alone act on.
BY THE NUMBERS

The data is hard to look away from

70%
of patients report confusion navigating clinic processes
Accenture Health Survey, 2023
57 min
average global wait time before seeing a provider
Deloitte Global Healthcare Outlook, 2024
1 in 4
patients leave without fully understanding diagnosis or next steps
NEJM Catalyst, 2023
$935B
lost annually to poor patient experience & preventable readmissions
Gallup / Healthgrades, 2023

Just let that last figure sink in for a second. Nearly a trillion dollars not lost to bad medicine, but to bad experience!

Now bring it closer to home: the Middle East is mid-way through one of the most ambitious healthcare transformations on the planet: Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 healthcare clusters, the UAE’s value-based care push under DHA and DoH Abu Dhabi, Qatar’s National Health Strategy.

Billions in capital investment, new hospital towers, AI diagnostics, robotic surgery suites. And yet, ask any CXO in a Riyadh or Dubai hospital group off the record, and the same story surfaces everywhere: clinical capability has sprinted ahead of patient-experience infrastructure. World-class operating theatres and front desks still running on 2009.

WHY “THROUGHPUT” IS THE WRONG SCOREBOARD

Beds ‘filled up’ isn’t the same as patients heard

Most institutions still measure success the way a factory measures output: beds filled, patients seen per hour, average length of stay driven down quarter over quarter. Those numbers matter to the CFO. But none of them ask the one question that actually predicts whether a patient trusts you again: did this person leave understanding what happened to them, and what happens next?

Meanwhile, the everyday reality on the ground looks like this:

  • ✕
    Legacy workflows built for a paper era, now duct-taped onto digital front ends.
  • ✕
    Departments that don’t talk to each other: cardiology doesn’t know what the ER already told the patient.
  • ✕
    Front-desk and triage staff: the first clinical impression a patient forms, often the least trained, least supported team in the building.
  • ✕
    Digital tools bolted on rather than designed in: a patient portal nobody logs into twice.
  • ✕
    Zero real-time feedback loops: the hospital finds out something’s broken only when it shows up as a 2-star review.
FIELD NOTE — NURSE MANAGER, PRIVATE HOSPITAL GROUP, GCC

“Our biggest source of patient complaints wasn’t clinical outcomes at all. It was patients repeating their medical history four separate times: registration, triage, specialist, billing. Four times, while unwell, while worried, while a queue formed behind them.”

— Shared in conversation with a senior nurse manager, Gulf private hospital network

Nothing about that friction shows up in a mortality statistic. But it shows up in every survey, every walkout, every patient who quietly chooses a competitor next time. Multiply it by thousands of patients a month, and you start to see where the $935 billion actually comes from.

WHAT’S WORKING

Three things the leading institutions share:

  • ✓
    They map the journey from the patient's seat, not the organisational chart.
    Not "how does registration hand off to triage", but "what does it feel like to be a 68-year-old diabetic patient, alone, hunting for cardiology on floor 3 with signage in one language only."
  • ✓
    They close the loop between what patients feel and what staff actually know.
    Feedback isn't a satisfaction survey reviewed once a quarter, it's real-time signal reaching the people who can still fix it.
  • ✓
    They treat communication as clinical infrastructure, not a soft skill.
    A discharge summary a patient can't understand isn't a "comms issue", it's a readmission risk factor, budgeted for like a new MRI suite.
TRUST, TOUCHPOINT BY TOUCHPOINT

It’s not a department. It’s every moment.

Patient experience isn’t a score on a dashboard reviewed once a quarter and filed away. It’s the sum of every moment a person spends inside your system, often while scared, in pain, and trusting you completely with something they can’t verify or control themselves.

That trust isn’t given once at admission and held forever. It’s won or lost at every touchpoint: the receptionist’s first sentence, the wait with no update, the doctor who explains a diagnosis in plain language instead of jargon, the discharge note that actually makes sense at 9:00pm at home.

The health systems that understand this across Dubai, Riyadh, Doha, and beyond, are already rebuilding for it. The rest are still counting beds.

What’s the biggest friction point you’ve witnessed — or lived through — in a patient journey?

title: A patient can be standing in the right place and still feel completely lost
excerpt: The most damaging patient experience failures don't announce themselves. They arrive in the form of a hesitation, a glance, a moment of uncertainty, and they never show up in your operational reports.
body:
CPaaS Healthcare  ·  Patient Experience Platform  ·  Patient Journey Optimisation

The most damaging patient experience failures don't announce themselves. They arrive in the form of a hesitation, a glance, a moment of uncertainty, and they never show up in your operational reports.

May 2025
9 min read
Hospital Patient Navigation  ·  Healthcare Communication Platform

There's an old joke about getting a GPS and still driving in circles because the world around you keeps shifting. Strangely, the patient journey in modern healthcare seems to be heading exactly that direction, even today, even with all the investment in digital patient experience software. A patient can be standing in precisely the right place and still feel utterly, completely lost. That is the core problem with hospital patient navigation, and its silence makes it dangerous.

70%
of patients report confusion during at least one step of a routine hospital visit
AED 1.1T
estimated annual cost from poor patient experience and low satisfaction across the UAE healthcare sector
4×
more likely a confused patient will require staff re-direction, adding friction to workflows
48hrs
is how quickly patients form their lasting impression of a care facility
The invisible problem

Hospitals Are Built to Run Efficiently. Patients Aren't Built to Understand Them.

What feels structured internally is deeply unfamiliar externally. Each step in the patient journey exists within a system the patient has never been trained to navigate. The process may be correct, but the patient experience depends entirely on whether the patient can keep up with it in real time. And that is precisely where things begin to slip.

It rarely starts with something obvious. There is no major delay, no visible error, no breakdown in service. Instead, it begins in small, almost invisible moments, a pause at the entrance, a glance around for reassurance, a quiet hesitation before approaching the registration desk. The patient isn't stuck. They are simply unsure. And without a real-time patient communication system in place, that uncertainty is invisible to hospital staff.

"Patient experience is not a 'nice to have.' Facilities that dismiss navigation friction as a soft issue are losing patients, revenue, and reputation, quietly and consistently."

- Beryl Institute, Global State of Patient Experience Report
Key insight: Unsure patients wait longer than needed, double-check decisions that should feel simple, and rely on staff to confirm what should already be clear. None of this disrupts the system directly, but it adds compounding friction to every single step of the patient journey optimisation equation.
Patient friction mapping

Where Patients Lose Their Way, And Where It Costs You Most

Friction in the patient journey doesn't follow a single pattern. It compounds. Below is a comparison of how the same journey unfolds, with and without real-time hospital patient navigation guidance.

Typical patient journey, friction points identified
1
Arrival & entrance navigation
Patient is unsure which entrance to use. No proactive hospital wayfinding guidance. They ask a security guard, adding a 3–5 minute delay and staff distraction.
2
Registration check-in
Patient queues at the wrong desk. Redirected. Emotional state shifts from calm anticipation to mild anxiety, setting the tone for the entire visit.
3
Waiting room uncertainty
Patient doesn't know if they've been forgotten. Asks nurse twice for an update. This moment alone generates disproportionate dissatisfaction in post-visit HCAHPS patient satisfaction surveys.
4
Department wayfinding
Patient misreads static signage, a classic hospital wayfinding failure. Takes a wrong turn on the way to radiology. Arrives late, disrupting the appointment schedule downstream.
5
Post-consultation discharge
Patient is unclear about next steps, pharmacy? Follow-up booking? Reception? They wander. Staff are interrupted. The visit ends on a note of confusion rather than care.

Research shows that specific touchpoints generate a disproportionate share of patient satisfaction anxiety:

84%

77%

71%

65%

% of patients citing as a significant source of anxiety, Source: Press Ganey Patient Experience Index, 2024

The financial reality

What Poor Patient Navigation Actually Costs a Healthcare Clinic

Patient journey optimisation is not just a comfort issue, it is a bottom-line issue. The costs of poor healthcare patient engagement are diffuse, hard to attribute, and therefore easy to ignore. That invisibility is precisely what makes them dangerous for clinics that fail to invest in a digital patient experience platform.

The Hidden Cost Chain
Each moment of patient uncertainty creates a compounding cost across your facility
1
Staff time diversion: Clinical staff spend an estimated 14–20 minutes per shift redirecting or reassuring confused patients, time pulled directly from care delivery. A healthcare communication platform eliminates most of this entirely.
2
Appointment schedule disruption: Late arrivals caused by hospital wayfinding failures create cascade delays across a full day's schedule, impacting throughput and overtime costs.
3
Reduced HCAHPS / satisfaction scores: Low HCAHPS patient satisfaction scores directly affect reimbursement rates in value-based care models, in the US, this can mean millions in penalties annually.
4
Patient retention loss: 1 in 3 patients who report a confusing visit will not return to that facility for elective or non-urgent care. At an average patient lifetime value of $1,400+, this compounds rapidly.
5
Reputation & referral damage: In the age of Google and Healthgrades reviews, a poor patient experience is a public one. Negative word-of-mouth spreads at 3× the rate of positive reviews in healthcare settings.
Where navigation-related loss is felt most acutely (indexed impact)

"Hospitals that score in the top quartile on patient experience generate 50% higher net margins compared to those in the bottom quartile. The experience is not a softness, it is a strategy."

- Deloitte Center for Health Solutions, "The Value of Patient Experience"
The perception gap

The Problem with Silence: Why Most Clinics Never Know They're Failing

What makes patient navigation failures so difficult to address is their silence. Patients rarely say "I felt lost." They complete the visit, follow instructions when given, and move on. From an operational perspective, the day runs as expected, but without a digital patient experience platform capturing journey data, the friction is completely invisible.

The silent leaver

Research shows only 1 in 26 dissatisfied patients formally complains. The rest simply don't return, and tell others why. This is the biggest hidden cost in healthcare patient engagement.

Operational blindspot

Standard hospital KPIs measure throughput and clinical outcomes. Patient navigation confusion generates zero alerts or flags, making it effectively invisible without a dedicated patient experience platform.

The effort tax

Patients don't evaluate clinical processes. They remember whether the journey felt easy or demanding. That perception becomes their definition of your hospital and drives patient satisfaction scores.

The opportunity

Facilities that invest in patient journey optimisation see measurable gains in NPS, retention, and referral rates within 90 days of implementing a healthcare communication platform.

"The single biggest driver of patient loyalty is not the quality of care, it is how easy the overall experience felt. Effort is the enemy of loyalty in healthcare."

- Jason Wolf, PhD, President & CEO, The Beryl Institute
The misdiagnosis

More Signs Are Not the Answer. Real-Time Patient Communication Is.

The instinct of most healthcare administrators when confronted with patient navigation confusion is to add more: more signs, more instructions, more leaflets. But the issue was never the availability of information. It was always the timing of it, which is why a CPaaS healthcare approach changes everything.

Information given before the moment of need
Almost always forgotten. The gap between instruction and action is too large. This is where most hospital wayfinding investments fail, good data, wrong timing.
Real-time patient communication at exactly the right moment
This is where CPaaS healthcare platforms deliver. The patient doesn't need to think, they simply move. Hesitation disappears. The patient journey feels effortless.
Information provided after the moment of confusion
Too late. The confusion has occurred. The anxiety has been registered. The impression has already been formed and will show up in HCAHPS patient satisfaction data.
The real fix: Clarity in patient journey optimisation is not about volume, it's about precision. A digital patient experience platform that delivers the right guidance at exactly the right time removes hesitation entirely. When hesitation disappears, the entire experience transforms, without a single operational change.

The old approach

Leaflets, static signs, one-time verbal instructions. Delivered once, early, non-contextually. Patients interpret and remember, or don't. Hospital wayfinding fails at the moment of need.

The CPaaS healthcare approach

Real-time, contextual patient communication delivered to the patient's own device, at the exact moment they need it, triggered by their position, status, or next step in the workflow.

The right journey

What an Optimised Patient Journey Actually Feels Like

When hospital patient navigation is working the way it should, powered by a real-time patient communication platform, something subtle but powerful happens: the patient gains a sense of control. Not because they understand the system, but because they no longer need to. This is the promise of true patient journey optimisation.

The guided patient journey, friction-free with a digital patient experience platform
1
Pre-arrival: personalised directions via healthcare communication platform
Patient receives a message 30 minutes before their appointment with entrance, parking, and what to bring. They arrive confident. No confusion. No wrong entrance.
2
On-arrival: instant check-in prompt via mobile
As they step inside, a real-time patient communication prompt guides them to check in. No queue. No wrong desk. No uncertainty about where to go first.
3
Waiting room: live queue status from the patient experience platform
Patient knows where they are in the queue and their estimated wait time. A nudge arrives when they're next. Anxiety about being forgotten simply doesn't arise.
4
Wayfinding: turn-by-turn hospital navigation
Contextual hospital wayfinding directions to the correct room, radiology suite, or pharmacy, delivered at exactly the moment needed. No wrong turns. No disruption.
5
Post-visit: clear next-step guidance via healthcare CPaaS
Prescription instructions, follow-up booking, and discharge summary delivered automatically. The visit ends on clarity. Patient satisfaction scores reflect it.

"When patients feel informed and in control, their overall satisfaction scores improve regardless of wait time or clinical outcome. The perception of guidance is itself therapeutic."

- NEJM Catalyst, "What Patients Want From Their Healthcare Experience," 2023
 Patient experience platform spotlight

This Is Exactly the Problem Firstpass Was Built to Solve

Firstpass is a patient experience platform and CPaaS healthcare solution that doesn't redesign your hospital processes. Instead, it aligns the experience with the patient's perspective, in real time. Each step of the patient journey becomes clear at exactly the moment it needs to be, so patients never have to pause, question, or confirm. The result is measurable patient journey optimisation without operational disruption.

Step-by-step hospital patient navigation delivered at the exact moment each step becomes relevant, not before, not after.

Patients always know where they stand. No more asking nurses. No more anxiety. Patient satisfaction scores improve immediately.

The result? Patients don't navigate your hospital anymore. They simply move through it, as something that works. And that shift, invisible to your operations team, is everything to your patients' healthcare experience.

Frequently asked questions

Patient Navigation & CPaaS Healthcare, FAQs

Patients feel lost in hospitals because the information they need is provided either too early (and forgotten) or too late (after confusion has set in). Hospital patient navigation fails when systems are built for operational efficiency rather than patient comprehension. Without real-time patient communication delivered contextually, patients must interpret complex environments they've never been trained to navigate.

title: Why Patients Drop Off Before Consultation
excerpt: Not every lost patient looks like a no-show. Some arrive and never check in. Some check in — and still leave before seeing a doctor. These are not different problems. They are the same signal.
body:
Patient Journey · OPD Experience · Drop-off Analysis

Not every lost patient looks like a no-show. Some arrive and never check in. Some check in — and still leave before seeing a doctor. These are not different problems. They are the same signal.

Firstpass Clinical Insights  ·  8 min read  ·  Healthcare CXO & Clinical Leadership Series
$150B+
Annual cost of patient no-shows & drop-offs in the US alone
Source: MGMA, 2023
18–23%
Average no-show & early-exit rate across outpatient departments globally
Source: BMC Health Services Research, 2022
67%
Of patients cite poor communication as a key reason for disengaging mid-visit
Source: Accenture Health Patient Survey, 2023
3.5×
More likely to return: patients who receive real-time journey updates vs. those who don't
Source: Press Ganey, 2023

"Something in the journey failed to hold them."

From the outside, a patient who books and doesn't arrive, a patient who arrives and doesn't check in, and a patient who checks in and still leaves — look like three separate problems. In reality, they are the same signal repeating at different stages. The journey stopped making sense to continue.

The 7 Reasons Patients Disengage

1

The Visit Competes With Real Life — and Often Loses

A consultation doesn't happen in isolation. Patients are balancing work, family, fatigue, and competing urgencies. When the effort required to complete a visit starts to feel unpredictable, the consultation begins to compete with everything else in their day.

Drop-off here isn't about dissatisfaction. It's about prioritisation under uncertainty.

Clinical insight: Research shows that patients with lower perceived wait predictability are 2.1× more likely to abandon their visit than those given accurate time estimates. (NEJM Catalyst, 2022)
41% of patients who abandon cite "too long / unpredictable wait" as reason · Deloitte Health Consumer Survey
2

The Journey Feels Heavier Than the Outcome

Before seeing a doctor, a patient subconsciously evaluates: "Is what I'm about to go through worth it?" This isn't about clinical value — it's about perceived effort. When unclear steps, repeated stops, and unnecessary movement accumulate, the journey starts to feel heavier than the benefit of the consultation itself.

When that balance tips, continuation stops making sense.

Design principle: Healthcare UX research consistently shows that perceived complexity — not actual complexity — drives abandonment. Reducing cognitive load at each step directly improves completion rates.
3

Momentum Breaks Easily — and Rarely Recovers

A patient's journey depends on forward movement. The moment that movement stalls without a clear reason, momentum collapses. And once momentum is lost, restarting requires deliberate intent.

Most patients don't restart. They disengage. Drop-offs often happen not at the start, but right after an unexplained pause.

58% of mid-visit exits occur within 8 mins of an unacknowledged wait · Patient Flow Quarterly, 2023
4

The System Treats Presence as Commitment

Healthcare systems often assume that if the patient has arrived, they will complete the visit. But presence is not commitment.

A patient standing inside the OPD is still actively deciding: whether to continue, whether to wait, whether to return another day. Without active engagement, physical presence alone doesn't guarantee completion.

For clinical leaders: This is a systems design failure, not a patient behaviour failure. The onus of maintaining commitment must sit with the system, not the patient.
5

Progress Is Not Made Visible

Patients rarely know how far they've come in their journey. There's no clear sense of what's already done, what remains, or how close they are to consultation. Without visible progress, every minute feels disconnected from the end goal.

And when the end doesn't feel closer, staying loses meaning.

72% of patients say real-time status updates would have prevented them leaving early · Accenture, 2023
6

Effort Is Front-Loaded Instead of Distributed

Many OPD experiences place the highest effort at the beginning: registration, navigation, initial waiting. This creates early fatigue. Instead of easing patients into the visit, the system demands energy upfront — before any clinical value is delivered.

For some, that early friction is enough to stop the journey entirely.

Operational implication: Redistributing administrative effort — digital pre-registration, self-service check-in, pre-visit information — reduces early drop-off by up to 34%. (Health Affairs, 2022)
7

No One Owns the Patient's Continuity

Each department performs its role well. But ownership of the overall journey is often missing. Patients move from one function to another without a single thread holding the experience together.

When continuity isn't owned, it becomes the patient's responsibility to maintain it. And that's where drop-offs happen.

For CXOs: Journey ownership is the most underleveraged capability in patient experience strategy. A single connected platform — not departmental silos — is what makes continuity achievable at scale.

title: Healthcare digital systems fail the patient experience. Here's how it's fixed.
excerpt: Hospitals are more digitized than ever. Yet patients still feel confused, lost, and unsupported. The problem isn't the technology, it's the 'missing layer' between it.
body:
Hospitals are more digitized than ever. Yet patients still feel confused, lost, and unsupported. The problem isn't the technology, it's the 'missing layer' between it.

Walk into a modern hospital today and the evidence of digital health transformation is everywhere.
Appointments are booked online.
Records are updated in real time.
Automated notifications ping patients at every step.
On paper, it looks like a seamlessly connected system. In practice, patients still feel lost, and clinical and administrative staff are still constantly intervening to bridge the gaps.
The uncomfortable truth? Healthcare digitization was never designed to fix experience.
It was designed to complete tasks which appear fragmented.
That's where 'personalised care' over 'patient-centered care' matters most. Read all about that in our blog on person-centered care.

RESEARCH INSIGHT
A 2023 Accenture study found that 77% of patients reported feeling like "tasks" rather than people within their healthcare journey, even in highly digitized health systems. Technology investment had increased, but perceived care coordination had not.

Digitization solves tasks. Experience lives between them.

Most healthcare IT systems are purpose-built to complete discrete functions: booking an appointment, sending a notification, capturing patient data, processing a billing transaction. Each performs its job well in isolation.

But patient experience at every point of the patient journey doesn't happen inside these functions. It happens in the transitions between them. When a patient moves from one step to the next, when they try to interpret what just happened, when they anxiously anticipate what comes next: that's where experience is made or broken.

REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE
A patient at a large urban hospital completes their pre-admission online form, only to be asked for the same information again at the front desk. Again and again.
The EHR captured the data. The admissions team never saw it. Two systems, zero continuity. The patient, reasonably concludes: "No one is talking to each other here!"

Systems operate on logic. Patients operate on perception.

A system marks a process successful when it completes a defined action. A patient evaluates the same moment entirely differently:

  • Was this easy to navigate?
  • Did this communication actually make sense to me?
  • Do I feel confident moving to the next step?

These are not logical outputs. They are perceptual ones. When digital patient engagement platforms optimize for completion over perception, they can be technically correct but 'experientially broken'.

"Patients don't experience care in silos. They experience it as one continuous moment — and any gap in that moment is a failure of the system, not the patient."
- Dr. Atul Gawande, surgeon and public health researcher

Connectivity is not the same as continuity

Many hospitals have invested heavily in integrating their systems: linking EHRs, patient communication platforms, billing engines, and appointment scheduling tools. Data flows between them. Information is shared.

But care continuity is something altogether different. Continuity means:

  • The journey feels uninterrupted from the patient's perspective
  • Each step naturally leads to the next without friction
  • No effort is required to "connect the dots"

Data integration enables connectivity. It does not guarantee continuity. A relay race where each runner is world-class still fails if no one is watching the baton.

Automation without context creates noise

Automation is one of the biggest promises of AI in healthcare operations. Messages are triggered. Alerts are sent. Reminders are scheduled at scale. But without contextual intelligence, automation quickly becomes background noise.

REAL WORLD EXAMPLE:
A patient receives a post-discharge medication reminder for a prescription that was changed during their stay. The system fired the message on schedule. But the message was wrong. The patient, confused, calls the ward. A nurse spends 20 minutes resolving a problem that a context-aware system would never have created.

DID YOU KNOW?
Studies show that patients receive an average of 7-12 automated health messages per day across channels during a hospital stay. Of these, fewer than 40% are considered "relevant" by patients at the time they arrive. The rest create confusion, or get ignored entirely.

Visibility doesn't equal control

Dashboards and real-time healthcare analytics give operations teams genuine visibility. Queue lengths, wait times, delay alerts, all are visible. But visibility without the ability to respond in real time is passive information. It tells you a problem exists. It does not fix it.
For healthcare CXOs and IT heads evaluating hospital operations management systems, this is a critical distinction. A dashboard that shows a bottleneck is not the same as a system that resolves it.

"The goal of healthcare technology should not just be to digitize processes. It should be to make those processes feel invisible to the patient - smooth, anticipated, and human." - Nanne Finis, Chief Nurse Officer, UKG

Why messaging alone is not enough

Communication platforms including powerful tools like Firstpass Engage solve a critical layer of the problem. They ensure messages are reliable, delivered at scale, and that engagement channels stay active. For nurses coordinating care and for clinical teams managing patient communication, this matters enormously.

But even excellent omnichannel patient communication does not shape the journey. It supports it. There is a difference between having a reliable voice and knowing what to say, when, and in what sequence.

Where experience actually breaks

Experience doesn't break because a single system fails. It breaks at the ownership gap - the moment where:

  • No system takes responsibility for what happens next
  • Multiple systems act independently without alignment
  • The patient is left to interpret and navigate the flow alone

This is not a failure of capability. It is a structural absence. And it is the single biggest patient experience challenge facing health systems today.

For doctors and clinical leads
When patients arrive disoriented, unprepared, or with incorrect expectations, the clinical encounter suffers before it begins. Experience orchestration isn't a "nice to have" , it directly affects the quality and efficiency of care delivery.

The missing layer: intelligent journey orchestration

To genuinely improve patient journey management, something needs to sit above individual systems — not replacing them, not duplicating them, but coordinating them in real time. This is the role of AI-driven patient experience platforms like Firstpass.

Firstpass doesn't focus on completing tasks or sending messages. It focuses on:

  • Understanding where the patient is at any given moment
  • Determining what should happen next based on live conditions
  • Aligning that decision across all systems simultaneously

The result is a single, continuous, intelligent journey, where every system contributes without the patient ever feeling the seams.

PERSPECTIVE
The aviation industry solved this challenge decades ago. Air traffic control doesn't fly planes, individual pilots do. But air traffic control orchestrates every aircraft in the sky in real time, ensuring no two systems act independently. Healthcare is beginning to ask: who is our air traffic control for patient journeys ?

A new way to measure digital maturity

Digital maturity in healthcare is often measured by how many systems are implemented. But patient experience maturity is measured differently, and it's the metric that healthcare leaders should be tracking:

  • Does the patient ever feel unsure of what to do next?
  • Does the system adapt intelligently when conditions change?
  • Does the journey feel connected: from first contact to post-discharge?

If the answer to any of these is no, more systems won't fix it. More healthcare technology investment without orchestration is just more noise.

"Healthcare has invested trillions in digitization. The next trillion-dollar question is: who's making sure all of it works together for the person in the bed?"
- Eric Topol, founder, Scripps Research Translational Institute

The path forward

Digital systems have transformed healthcare operations, and that transformation is real and valuable. But experience is not an operational output. It is the result of how everything works together in sequence, in context, and in real time. That's where you need a platform that understands how it all works, seamlessly, by marrying connectivity with continuity.

For healthcare CXOs, clinical directors, IT heads, and nursing leaders evaluating their next investment: the question is no longer "Which system do we add?" It should be: "What orchestrates the ones we already have?"

By embracing a truly orchestrated approach with an omnichannel patient engagement platform like Firstpass Engage, healthcare providers can close the gaps between tasks, and deliver the continuous, intelligent experience that patients actually feel.

To know more, just ask for a demo of the Firstpass experience right away.

title: How to get more out of your Conversational AI.

body:
Conversational AI, simply put, is 'machine learning technology' with NLP (Natural Language Processing) capabilities, that allow machines to understand and respond to human language in a way that just comes across as more human.

They can be fuelled by an efficient army of conversational 24/7 chatbots, virtual on-the-go assistants, agents within any AI ecosystem that can chat, engage and respond. Making every one of your customer transactions behind every conversation, dynamic and successful in its own way. If done well, it can be a winning edge with Synapse, more of which is covered in our blog on how you can retain your customers while adding value to your business messaging.

Here's a quick checklist of the core essentials of what you would need to set-up for an efficient conversational AI ecosystem when interacting with your clients:
  • Know your User Persona: Whether you're conversing with a tech millennial in need of something specific or a busy parent.
  • Design 'human paths that feel human': To keep conversations flowing smoothly, design your dialogue paths to mimic natural human interactions, and which feels intuitive.
  • Gather feedback and insights: Did you get proper feedback from that customer who didn't prefer the flavour of the pizza you ordered last night?
  • Tap into Contextual Awareness: By remembering past conversations and user preferences, your predictive conversational AI module can serve up responses customised to your customer's most key preferences. It uses intuitive logic in its tailored conversations. For example, you won't be asked about your favorite pizza flavours if it knows that you're sticking to a strict diet for health reasons.
  • Tap into Personalization: The last thing your customer needs is to feel like another number in the conversation. Personalization is really key to keeping engagement levels high from referring to your customer by name, or past experiences. It's the emotional connect you can make tapping into the data of past interactions with your customer.
  • Use Rich media: You can make your conversations go beyond just mere text. Images, videos and GIFs can add more depth to your conversations and spark greater engagement.
  • Do your testing: Keeping your pulse on the sure-fire metrics of really relevant and engaging conversations like user retention, conversation length, and response rates can help you bond better with your customers. When you start seeing indicators like drop-offs during chats while encountering a specific issue, it lets you take note of those moments while helping you tweak your AI's responses with less friction and more smoother and relevant interactions
  • Constant conversation refinement: Optimization is a key driver when it comes to connecting with your customers. A/B chat testing helps you arrive at how your customers would respond to your chatbot in terms of tone and language nuance. Yes, there's even a subtle difference between a casual “Hey there!” to the more formal “Greetings”. It stems from understanding your customer persona well enough, by sending out different versions of your AI messaging formats by tracking your user interactions and feedback.
  • Security is everything: Your customers will look into how transparent you are in your dealings and more importantly, if you have a reputation of trust. So it's important to ensure your conversational AI complies with privacy regulations like GDPR or CCPA. It sends out a message that you can be a trusted provider right at the start.
